summary: Specifies how hosts can offer ISO transport services on top of TCP, reserving TCP port 102 for it. This is version 3 of the protocol and replaces RFC 983, with changes that are minor but incompatible. The RFC was an Internet standard and was later updated by RFC 2126.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1006 defines how ISO transport service can run over TCP instead of an ISO network protocol. It places each ISO transport unit inside a TPKT packet, whose header marks the packet's length in TCP's continuous stream. The specification reserves TCP port 102 for this service.

subtitle: How ISO transport messages are framed for exchange over a TCP connection.

tldr.problem: ISO session, presentation and application protocols needed a transport service while ISO's lower network layers were still developing. TCP already provided a transport service that could carry those applications.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1006 runs ISO transport class 0 over TCP port 102. A four-octet TPKT header gives each transport unit a length so the receiver can recover message boundaries from TCP's byte stream.
tldr.outcome: Version 3 of RFC 1006 is an Internet Standard. It obsoletes RFC 983, whose protocol it describes as slightly but incompatibly different, and RFC 2126 updates it.

today: RFC 1006 is an Internet Standard and specifies version 3. It obsoletes RFC 983 and has been updated by RFC 2126.

sections.title: ISO Transport Service over TCP
sections.content:
RFC 1006 specifies how a host can offer the ISO transport service using TCP and IP underneath. The aim was to let ISO and CCITT session, presentation and application protocols run in the Internet without changing those higher layers. The ISO transport service access point (TSAP) remains the interface presented to those applications.

The protocol uses ISO transport class 0 over a TCP connection rather than over an ISO network protocol. The RFC calls this version 3 and says it supersedes RFC 983; the changes are minor but incompatible. It reserves TCP port 102 for hosts implementing the service.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 1006 lets applications that expect ISO transport service use TCP underneath. The applications keep the ISO interface, while the host carries their transport messages over a TCP connection on port 102.

sections.title: Why the Transport Layer Is the Boundary
sections.content:
The RFC's motivation is to make higher-level ISO protocols available before mature ISO lower-layer implementations are ready. TCP/IP already offers transport and internetwork services, so it can support development and use of those higher-level protocols.

The memo places the connection between the suites at the transport service access point. It explicitly says it is not a migration or interception plan; any overall transition plan is outside its scope. The document focuses on providing the service described in the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC uses TCP because it can provide the lower-level service while ISO applications are being developed. It defines a transport connection, not a plan for moving an entire network from TCP/IP to ISO.

sections.title: The Transport Service and TCP Connection
sections.content:
A TS-user is a process that uses transport service, and a TS-peer implements the protocol described by the RFC. The TS-provider offers the ISO TSAP interface above and uses TCP below. Quality of Service parameters are not supported and are left for further study.

The ISO service is symmetric; it does not define a client/server model. A TCP listener accepts a connection, after which the provider indicates the incoming connection to the TS-user. TCP connection, data-ready, close and error events are mapped to the ISO transport service's connect, data and disconnect events.
sections.plainLanguage: A program uses the familiar ISO transport interface, and the provider translates its requests into TCP operations. When a TCP connection arrives, the provider reports it to the waiting ISO application.

sections.title: Connecting and Transferring Data
sections.content:
A TS-peer opens a TCP connection to the other host's address on port 102. A server listens on that port and accepts the connection. The default TPDU size is 65531 octets; a smaller standard size can be negotiated using ISO 8073's mechanism. Expedited data is disabled by default and may be negotiated during connection setup.

For data transfer, the peer places each transport protocol data unit (TPDU) in a TPKT and sends it through TCP. If expedited data was negotiated, a modified expedited-data TPDU travels on the same TCP connection. Releasing the transport connection closes TCP; a TCP close or error becomes a transport disconnect indication.
sections.plainLanguage: The peers connect over TCP port 102 and exchange TPKTs, each carrying an ISO transport unit. Expedited data is optional and, if agreed, uses the same TCP connection as ordinary data.

sections.title: The TPKT Packet Header
sections.content:
TCP provides a stream of octets without message boundaries, while ISO transport class 0 expects separate units. RFC 1006 frames each TPDU as one TPKT, consisting of a fixed four-octet header followed by the TPDU.

The header contains an 8-bit version field, a reserved octet and a 16-bit packet length. The version is 3. Packet length counts the header and the TPDU, and ranges from 7 to 65535 octets. This allows a maximum TPDU size of 65531 octets and a maximum TSDU size of 65524 octets. An expedited transport service data unit is limited to 16 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: The TPKT header tells the receiver where each transport unit ends in TCP's byte stream. It includes the version and total packet length, followed by one ISO transport unit.

sections.title: Version History and Earlier Specification
sections.content:
RFC 1006 records that experience with RFC 983 led to versions 2 and 3. The authors observed that the protocol was close to ISO transport class 0 and described the design as a way to encapsulate that protocol inside TCP.

The RFC says the changes between versions were relatively small, while warning that the changes from RFC 983 are incompatible. Its status information identifies version 3 and states that RFC 983 is superseded.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 1006 is the third version of the specification and replaces RFC 983. The authors describe it as a way to carry ISO transport class 0 inside TCP, while warning that the earlier version is not compatible.
